contentHtml:
Hitesh Goswami, CEO and Co-Founder, 4baseCare, discusses the need to bridge gaps in access to genomic testing, the role of technology and collaboration in taking precision oncology beyond major urban centres, and the steps needed to integrate genomics into routine cancer care across India

Over the last decade, cancer care has entered a new era where treatment decisions are becoming much more personalized and targeted. This has led to significant improvements in clinical outcomes while enhancing the quality of life of patients. Despite many of these technological advances in genomics, the access to these innovations are centred around urban cities. Hospitals in cities like Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi have integrated genomic testing as a part of cancer care, but patients in Tier II and III cities continue to face barriers such as lack of diagnostic infrastructure, shortage of specialist expertise and cumbersome long-distance travel to access advanced cancer care. Due to these challenges, many patients end up receiving cancer care that may not be the most ideal for their genetic profile.

Currently, the real challenge is not building better science, it’s about making our scientific inventions accessible to the masses. We need a bridge that carries our science from the lab into every cancer treating hospital across the country. We need to create an ecosystem that enables every patient, irrespective of their city, to benefit from advanced cancer care.

Bringing genomics-driven care closer to the patient

A hospital in a small town in Kerala now provides advanced genetic testing to cancer patients, serving not only the town but also neighbouring regions. Their approach was straightforward. The hospital built a collaborative ecosystem by partnering with genomic experts who could bring advanced genetic testing to where the patients are.

The key takeaway from the above example is that the approach towards the delivery of advanced cancer diagnostics requires a fundamental shift in thinking. We can no longer expect patients to travel long-distances to access advanced cancer care. We need to find ways to integrate genomics into existing systems to make it easily accessible to patients. Building partnerships with technology providers, hospitals and research institutions can go a long way in making genomics-led cancer truly accessible.

The impact it has

Bringing cutting-edge genomic technologies to where the patient is not only makes it more convenient but also improves patient outcomes. Genomics driven cancer care allows oncologists to access timely molecular insights that support more informed treatment decisions. For example, in the case of lung cancer, it helps identify specific genetic alterations, such as EGFR or ALK mutations, that helps clinicians prescribe targeted therapies instead of relying on one-size-fits-all approaches. This not only increases chances of treatment success but also helps patients avoid unnecessary toxicity and the financial burden of therapies that may not be very effective.

The real value of genomics goes beyond generating genetic information. It lies in the accurate interpretation of complex molecular data points and translating those numbers into actionable insights that can turn into clinical decisions. This is where artificial intelligence can play a role. A collaborative ecosystem with hospitals and precision oncology companies will allow oncologists to gain deeper insights from genomic and clinical data. AI-powered platforms can analyse a patient’s unique molecular profile against large-scale, real-world datasets comprising treatment responses and patient outcomes. This helps oncologists to decide on specific treatment that can work for the patient, predict the likelihood of response to specific therapies, and make evidence-based treatment decisions

Collaboration is the way forward

Democratizing access to genomic innovation cannot be achieved by a single stakeholder. It needs a collaborative ecosystem where healthcare institutions, precision oncology companies, oncologists and policymakers have to come together to address the existing gaps. While expanding access is one side of the story, creating a pool of skilled oncology workforce who can understand genomic data and derive insights from it is yet another area that needs attention. In addition, to make the entire ecosystem grow, we need supportive policy frameworks that can integrate genomic testing into routine cancer care. Only through coordinated efforts across all these fronts can precision oncology move beyond a few urban centres and become accessible to patients in even the smallest towns across the country.
